newsitem.title: ROMANIA: High turnout in Romanian general election.
newsitem.headline: High turnout in Romanian general election.

text.p: Romanians flocked to polling stations on Sunday to choose between President Ion Iliescu's moderate post-Communist reforms and the centrist opposition's pledge of swift action to tackle widespread poverty.
With turnout at just over 70 percent, state television said some polling stations would stay open until midnight (2200 GMT), three hours longer than scheduled, to cater for a late surge of voters.

Exit polls are due after the close of voting. But local analysts said it was uncertain how accurately they would match official results, due to start trickling in on Monday. They also suggested there could be a high number of spoiled ballots.
Iliescu, 66, one of 16 candidates for president, has been in office since taking charge of Romania in the aftermath of the 1989 revolution that ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

Despite jibes that he has done little to end communist-era decay, he held a slender lead in opinion polls over academic Emil Constantinescu, 56, leader of the Democratic Convention and former Prime Minister Petre Roman, 50.
A run-off between the top two finishers is almost certain later this month.
The high turnout is thought to favour Iliescu. But a beaming Constantinescu told reporters on Sunday evening he was "very optimistic" about the outcome.
"I will vote for Iliescu because I know him best," said Nela Mocanu, 31, one of only a handful of voters on Bucharest streets openly admitting their support for the president.
Iliescu portrays his opponents as risk-takers and himself as a guarantor of stability able to avoid the more dramatic economic slide of Bulgaria and ethnic conflicts of Yugoslavia.
Even if he does win, Iliescu could face a hostile parliament as his Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), tainted by corruption scandals, trails in parliamentary elections.

Reports of voting irregularities poured in throughout the day, with one Romanian watchdog organisation urging parties to lodge formal complaints. Opposition parties had said during the campaign that Iliescu's PDSR was planning mass fraud.

Thousands of voters left off official registers were allowed to vote on "special lists" and television reported entire buildings omitted from records. About 13 percent of all ballots were invalidated in the 1992 general election.

Many of the 17 million voters appear disgusted at soaring prices, charges of ruling party incompetence and an economic slump that has pushed living standards well below those of Hungary, Poland, and the Czech Republic.
"I want a better life for my family," said Grigore Vasile, 40, a rail worker in the resort of Sinaia, north of Bucharest. "I want new faces. Seven years with the same people is enough."
City voters, hardest hit by industrial decline, appear particularly distrustful of the president, who has come to rely on rural areas for his support.
"I regard these elections as a normalisation of the general climate and the general political development of our country," Iliescu told Reuters after he and his wife Nina voted.
His comments were directed at Western suspicions of the democratic credentials of his administration.
Romania's campaign to join NATO and the European Union depends on a free and fair election. It is the only east European state where anti-communists have not been in power.
Iliescu's rivals offer tax cuts, honest government and faster reforms and pledge to shun any coalition with the PDSR.
